slides: Open by presenting the five Platonic solids as the rare intersection of topology, metric regularity, and symmetry. Euler's formula alone is not enough; the lecture will keep asking which counts, angles, radii, and reciprocal relationships force exactly these five solids.

Use the route slide to prevent the chapter from becoming a picture gallery. The sequence starts with pyramid, prism, and antiprism families, then compares drawing methods, derives Euler symbol constraints, inspects the five mesh counts, measures radii and angles, studies reciprocal pairs, and ends by separating Euler from regularity.

The construction families slide gives students a controlled warm-up before the regular solids. Pentagonal pyramids, prisms, and antiprisms all have Euler characteristic two and watertight triangulations, but they are families rather than the highly constrained Platonic cases.

Drawings and models are not interchangeable records. A net records faces for building, a perspective model records spatial shape, and a Schlegel map records planar incidence. The slide asks students to keep these representations linked while recognizing what each one forgets.

Euler classification is the proof core of the chapter. The relations qV equals two E equals pF combine with V minus E plus F equals two to produce the denominator condition, and only five positive regular symbols survive before the flat and overfull cases appear.

The mesh gallery slide attaches the five symbols to actual topological data. Each solid has Euler characteristic two, equal edge lengths in the constructed model, and a watertight triangulation. The counts make the classification concrete rather than merely symbolic.

Radii and angles show that the five solids are metrically different even when the same Euler identity holds. Circumradius, midradius, inradius, angular defect, and dihedral angle change with the Schlaefli symbol, and the cube-octahedron values preview duality.

Reciprocal polyhedra turn faces into vertices and swap the Schlaefli parameters. Cube and octahedron form a dual pair, dodecahedron and icosahedron form another, and the tetrahedron is self-dual. Orthogonality checks show the face-center construction is geometrically aligned.

The regularity lab is a useful warning. A rectangular box still satisfies Euler's formula and has a reciprocal graph, but its edge lengths and face-center radii are unequal. This is the moment to separate topological sphere-like behavior from Platonic regularity.

Close by making the classification feel earned. The five solids arise because regular local face data, Euler topology, positive symbol counts, metric radii and angles, and reciprocal duality all agree. The artifacts are checks against that single coherent story.
